title: Which American Jobs Are Actually Growing?

segments.label: scene 1 (title)
segments.text: The American workforce is undergoing a historic, quiet transformation. While headlines focus on tech or factory floors, one sector is quietly dominating.

segments.label: scene 2 (counter)
segments.text: Private education and healthcare jobs have surged to an unprecedented 28.1 million today. This isn't just a trend; it is a total reshaping of the economy.

segments.label: scene 3 (line)
segments.text: Since 1990, this massive sector has grown by 160%. It is now 2.6 times larger than it was back then.

segments.label: scene 4 (statement)
segments.text: Healthcare and education are pulling ahead because our aging population and professional training needs show no signs of slowing down.

segments.label: scene 5 (compare)
segments.text: Compare this to manufacturing, which has seen a 29% decline since 1990. Automation and global shifts have fundamentally changed that landscape.

segments.label: scene 6 (line)
segments.text: Even the information sector remains largely flat compared to the early 2000s, barely holding onto its share of the total workforce.

segments.label: scene 7 (multiline)
segments.text: The surge in human-centric jobs is real. Let’s look at why these specific sectors are the true engines of modern employment.

segments.label: scene 8 (statement)
segments.text: To understand where we are, we have to look back at the workforce of 1990. It was a different era entirely.

segments.label: scene 9 (counter)
segments.text: Back then, manufacturing was the undeniable titan of the economy, employing 17.8 million people.

segments.label: scene 10 (line)
segments.text: It hit a peak of 17.9 million in February 1990, serving as the country's primary employment engine.

segments.label: scene 11 (counter)
segments.text: Meanwhile, the private education and health sector was just beginning its climb, starting at 10.8 million jobs.

segments.label: scene 12 (bars)
segments.text: According to the Bureau of Labor Statistics, construction and information sectors were much smaller pillars back then.

segments.label: scene 13 (slope)
segments.text: The landscape was defined by industrial output, with millions more working on factory floors than in classrooms or clinics.

segments.label: scene 14 (stacked)
segments.text: But the tide was already turning. The foundations of a service-oriented future were being quietly laid.

segments.label: scene 15 (statement)
segments.text: As the new millennium approached, the American economic bedrock began to shift.

segments.label: scene 16 (line)
segments.text: Manufacturing took the hardest hit, falling by 29% from its early 1990s peak.

segments.label: scene 17 (counter)
segments.text: By April 2020, factory employment reached a historic low of 11.4 million jobs.

segments.label: scene 18 (line)
segments.text: Meanwhile, the tech-heavy information sector saw a wild ride after the dot-com bubble burst.

segments.label: scene 19 (compare)
segments.text: From a peak of 3.72 million in 2001, information sector jobs fell by 26% by today.

segments.label: scene 20 (gauge)
segments.text: Volatility became the defining feature of the tech era, leaving total headcount largely stagnant.

segments.label: scene 21 (multiline)
segments.text: While these pillars faltered, the economy was silently preparing to transition toward human-centric roles.

segments.label: scene 22 (statement)
segments.text: Why is the economy shifting so dramatically? It starts with the people we care for.

segments.label: scene 23 (line)
segments.text: As the population ages, the demand for health and education services has exploded, climbing 160% since 1990.

segments.label: scene 24 (counter)
segments.text: Meanwhile, the construction sector is reaching new heights to meet modern infrastructure and housing needs.

segments.label: scene 25 (compare)
segments.text: Construction has grown by 54% since 1990, reflecting the physical expansion required by a changing nation.

segments.label: scene 26 (line)
segments.text: In contrast, the information sector has faced significant pressure, struggling to reclaim its turn-of-the-century footprint.

segments.label: scene 27 (gauge)
segments.text: Tech and information jobs have seen a 2% change since 1990, leaving employment levels relatively flat.

segments.label: scene 28 (slope)
segments.text: Our economy is trading industrial assembly for service-based care, rewriting the map of American work.

segments.label: scene 29 (kpi)
segments.text: To understand today's hiring momentum, we look at the last twelve months of job growth across four major sectors. The trends reveal a stark divide in the American labor market.

segments.label: scene 30 (compare)
segments.text: Private education and healthcare leads the pack with a 1.9% increase. It is the clear engine of modern hiring.

segments.label: scene 31 (line)
segments.text: Construction follows closely, growing by 1.5% as the nation continues to expand its physical infrastructure.

segments.label: scene 32 (statement)
segments.text: Manufacturing is showing modest signs of life, ticking upward by 0.6% over the last year.

segments.label: scene 33 (line)
segments.text: However, the information sector tells a very different story. It has contracted by 4.2% since last year.

segments.label: scene 34 (bars)
segments.text: Comparing these one-year changes highlights which industries are currently pulling away from the pack.

segments.label: scene 35 (slope)
segments.text: This snapshot defines the current labor climate, separating sectors experiencing active expansion from those undergoing painful rebalancing.

segments.label: scene 36 (statement)
segments.text: The American workforce is fundamentally different than it was just a few years ago. We are seeing a major shift toward service-centered employment.

segments.label: scene 37 (counter)
segments.text: Private education and healthcare now employ 28.1 million people. This sector has seen a 14% increase since 2020.

segments.label: scene 38 (line)
segments.text: In contrast, manufacturing has remained relatively flat. Employment sits at 12.7 million, showing a 1% decrease from 2020 levels.

segments.label: scene 39 (multiline)
segments.text: These two sectors tell the story of a modern economy prioritizing human services over traditional industrial output.

segments.label: scene 40 (kpi)
segments.text: The transition is clear: health, education, and services are the true pillars of growth today.

segments.label: scene 41 (statement)
segments.text: Have you noticed more new jobs or businesses opening in healthcare or education in your own town? Tell us in the comments.

segments.label: scene 42 (statement)
segments.text: If you want to keep tracking these trends, please subscribe to our channel for more data stories.
